target: पिताजी हर वीकेंड हमें पार्क ले जाते थे।
english: Father used to take us to the park every weekend.
tip: 'Take us to the park' = ले जाते थे (le jate the), literally take-go. Bringing back is ले आना (le aana = take-come). Direction lives in the second verb.

target: हम हर गर्मी में नानी के घर जाते थे।
english: We used to go to grandmother's house every summer.
tip: नानी के घर जाते थे (nani ke ghar jate the) = went to grandma's – घर (ghar) needs no word for 'to': 'grandma's home' alone is the destination.

target: गाँव के चौपाल पर हर शाम कहानियाँ सुनाई जाती थीं।
english: Stories used to be told every evening at the village meeting place.
tip: The passive is built on 'go': सुनाई जाती थीं (sunai jati theen) = used to be told, literally 'went being told'. Verb + जाना (jana) = passive.

target: जिस मकान में हम रहते थे, वह अब गिरा दिया गया।
english: The house in which we used to live has now been demolished.
tip: Hindi flips relative clauses: जिस मकान में हम रहते थे, वह (jis makaan mein hum rahte the, vah) = 'in which house we lived, THAT one'. The closing वह (vah) is required.

target: चिट्ठी लिखकर हालचाल पूछते थे।
english: People used to write letters asking about each other's well-being.
tip: No subject at all: पूछते थे (poochhte the) alone means 'people used to ask'. Hindi drops a generic 'people/one' – the verb ending carries it.

target: बचपन में दादी कहानियाँ सुनाती थीं।
english: In childhood, grandmother used to tell stories.
tip: 'Telling' stories = making them heard: सुनाती थीं (sunati theen) comes from सुनाना (sunana) – सुनना (sunna = hear) + make. Grandma made the stories heard.

target: सुरंग में ट्रेन चलती है।
english: The train runs through the tunnel.
tip: Trains walk in Hindi: ट्रेन चलती है (train chalti hai = the train walks). चलना (chalna) covers run, move, work – buses, machines, even watches चलते हैं (chalte hain).

target: ठेले पर गर्मागर्म जलेबी मिलती थी।
english: Hot jalebis were available on the cart.
tip: जलेबी मिलती थी (jalebi milti thi) – jalebis 'were gotten', not sold: मिलना (milna) means to be available or received. The same verb also means 'to meet'.

target: दूधवाला सुबह-सुबह दूध देने आता था।
english: The milkman used to come to deliver milk early morning.
tip: दूधवाला (doodhvala) = the milk one – वाला (vala) sticks to any noun and means 'the one with/of it': सब्ज़ीवाला (sabzivala), रिक्शावाला (rickshavala).

target: कबाड़ीवाला पुराने अख़बार ख़रीदने आता था।
english: The junk dealer used to come to buy old newspapers.
tip: 'Came to buy' = ख़रीदने आता था (kharidne aata tha) – purpose takes the -ने (-ne) form of the verb, with no word for 'to' at all.

target: पहले गाँवों में बिजली नहीं होती थी।
english: Earlier, villages did not have electricity.
tip: Villages don't 'have' electricity – Hindi says it 'is in' them: गाँवों में बिजली नहीं होती थी (gaanvon mein bijli nahin hoti thi). There is no verb for 'have'.

target: उन दिनों दीपक कोलकाता में रहता था।
english: In those days Deepak used to live in Kolkata.
tip: उन दिनों (un dinon) = in those days – no में (mein = in) needed. Time phrases in the -ों form work as 'in/during' on their own.

target: छुट्टियों में मामा के गाँव जाते थे।
english: During vacations we used to go to maternal uncle's village.
tip: मामा (mama) is only your mother's brother – dad's younger brother is चाचा (chacha), his elder ताऊ (tau). Hindi kinship always names the side.

target: सर्दियों में रज़ाई ओढ़कर कहानियाँ सुनते थे।
english: In winters we used to listen to stories wrapped in quilts.
tip: Quilts aren't worn, they're draped: रज़ाई ओढ़कर (razai odhkar). ओढ़ना (odhna) covers blankets and shawls; पहनना (pahnna) is for clothes on the body.

target: गर्मियों में कुल्फ़ीवाला गली-गली आवाज़ लगाता था।
english: In summers, the kulfi seller used to call out in every lane.
tip: गली-गली (gali-gali) = in every single lane – doubling a noun means 'each and every': घर-घर (ghar-ghar) = every house.

target: मेरे पापा पहले सिगरेट पीते थे।
english: My dad used to smoke.
tip: Hindi drinks cigarettes: सिगरेट पीते थे (cigarette peete the). पीना (peena) covers both drinking and smoking – there is no separate verb.

target: हम हर इतवार बाहर खाना खाते थे।
english: We used to eat out every Sunday.
tip: खाना खाते थे (khana khate the) = 'ate food' – खाना (khana) is both 'food' and 'to eat', so having a meal doubles it. Perfectly normal Hindi.

target: नहर में मछलियाँ पकड़ते थे हम बचपन में।
english: We used to catch fish in the canal in childhood.
tip: हम (hum = we) lands after the verb: पकड़ते थे हम (pakadte the hum) – spoken Hindi tosses known info behind the verb. Neutral order keeps the verb last.

target: नहर में कूदकर तैरने का मज़ा लेते थे।
english: We used to enjoy jumping and swimming in the canal.
tip: You take fun in Hindi, not have it: तैरने का मज़ा लेते थे (tairne ka maza lete the) = took the fun of swimming. Enjoying = मज़ा लेना (maza lena).

target: जब हम छोटे थे, तो मिट्टी में खेलते थे।
english: When we were small, we used to play in the mud.
tip: जब हम छोटे थे, तो (jab hum chhote the, to) = 'when we were small, then' – a जब (jab) clause usually opens its main clause with तो (to), which English never translates.

target: सुषमा समय पर आ जाती तो हम साथ चल सकते थे।
english: If Sushma had come on time, we could have gone together.
tip: आ जाती तो (aa jaati to) = 'had she come' – the unreal past drops था (tha) entirely. A bare -ती/-ता (-ti/-ta) verb signals 'if only it had happened'.

target: दीमक ने लकड़ी का फ़र्नीचर खा लिया।
english: Termites ate the wooden furniture.
tip: खा लिया (kha liya) = ate it UP – adding लेना (lena = take) marks an action as fully done. The दीमक (deemak = termites) didn't just eat, they finished the job.

target: भोर होते ही मुर्ग़ा बाँग देता था।
english: The rooster used to crow at dawn.
tip: भोर होते ही (bhor hote hi) = the instant dawn broke – verb in -ते (-te) + ही (hi) means 'as soon as'. Works anywhere: आते ही (aate hi) = right on arriving.

target: पतंगबाज़ी में हम सबसे आगे रहते थे।
english: We used to be ahead of everyone in kite flying.
tip: Superlatives compare against everyone: सबसे आगे (sabse aage) = 'ahead of all' = furthest ahead. सबसे (sabse) + adjective is how Hindi says '-est'.

target: आम के पेड़ पर चढ़कर कच्चे आम तोड़ते थे।
english: We used to climb mango trees and pick raw mangoes.
tip: कच्चे आम (kachche aam) = raw mangoes – कच्चा (kachcha) is one word for unripe, uncooked, unpaved, half-done. Its opposite पक्का (pakka) covers ripe, cooked, solid.

target: दीवार के पीछे एक बगीचा है।
english: There is a garden behind the wall.
tip: Position words follow the noun in Hindi: दीवार के पीछे (deewaar ke peechhe) is 'the wall behind' – the reverse of English 'behind the wall'.

target: अस्पताल पुणे के बीचोबीच है।
english: The hospital is right in the center of Pune.
tip: बीचोबीच (beechobeech) is बीच (beech = middle) doubled: पुणे के बीचोबीच (Pune ke beechobeech) = right in the center of Pune. Doubling adds the 'exactly'.

target: नरेश के पास पाँच सौ रुपये हैं।
english: Naresh has five hundred rupees.
tip: Hindi has no verb for 'have'. नरेश के पास (Naresh ke paas) is literally 'near Naresh' – so 'Naresh has 500 rupees' comes out as 'near Naresh are 500 rupees'.

target: ट्रेन पुल के ऊपर से गुज़रती है।
english: The train passes over the bridge.
tip: के ऊपर (ke oopar) alone means sitting on top. Motion across adds से (se): पुल के ऊपर से गुज़रती है (pul ke oopar se guzarti hai) = passes over the bridge.

target: क्या आपके पास शाकाहारी थाली है?
english: Do you have a vegetarian thali?
tip: With pronouns, के fuses in: आपके पास (aapke paas) = 'you have' – one word आपके (aapke), never आप के (aap ke). Same fusion in मेरे (mere) and उसके (uske).
